x:
An octopus is one of the best hiders in the ocean. In less than a second, it can change the color of its skin to match the rocks, sand, or coral around it. Tiny cells in its skin hold sacs of colored pigment, and muscles squeeze or stretch those sacs to make new patterns. Some octopuses can even make bumps on their skin so they look like rough stones.

Octopuses have other surprises too. Each one has three hearts and blue blood, and its eight arms are covered with suckers that can both touch and taste. When an octopus is in danger, it may squirt a cloud of dark ink and then shoot away. Scientists who study them say they are clever, curious, and very good at escaping from tanks.

Every fall, millions of monarch butterflies leave Canada and the eastern United States and fly south. Their trip can be close to 3,000 miles long, and it ends in the mountain forests of central Mexico. There, the butterflies cluster on fir trees so thickly that the branches look orange.

What makes this journey amazing is that no single monarch makes the whole round trip. In the spring, the butterflies head north, lay eggs on milkweed plants, and then die. Their children and grandchildren keep moving north, so it takes several generations to reach Canada again. Then a new group of butterflies, born at the end of summer, somehow finds its way back to the same forests in Mexico. Scientists think they use the sun to guide them, but they are still learning how it works.

Saturday, January 14

This morning I filled the bird feeder in our backyard, and then I sat by the kitchen window with my notebook. At first nothing happened, so I almost gave up. After ten minutes, a pair of cardinals landed on the fence. The male was bright red, but the female was a soft brown with red on her wings and tail.

Next, three chickadees came and grabbed seeds one at a time. They flew to a branch, cracked each seed, and came right back for more. Then a loud blue jay showed up and scared them all away. My grandpa told me that blue jays can copy the call of a hawk, which might be a trick to keep other birds away from the food. I counted nine birds in all, and I can't wait to try again next weekend.

Beavers are famous for their building skills. They cut down small trees with their strong front teeth, which never stop growing and are colored orange because they contain iron. Then they drag the branches to a stream and pile them up with mud and stones. Over time, the pile becomes a dam that slows the water and makes a pond.

The pond keeps the beavers safe. In the middle of it, they build a home called a lodge, and its entrances are hidden underwater where most predators can't reach. In winter, the beavers stay warm inside and swim out under the ice to eat bark from branches they stored earlier. Their dams also help other animals, because the new ponds and wetlands give homes to frogs, fish, ducks, and many insects.

Most substances get heavier for their size when they freeze, so their solid form sinks in their liquid form. Water is different. When water freezes, its molecules line up in a pattern that leaves more open space between them. That makes ice about nine percent less dense than liquid water, so ice cubes float to the top of your glass.

This odd fact matters a great deal for life on Earth. In winter, a lake freezes from the top down, and the layer of ice acts like a lid. It keeps the water below from losing heat too fast, so fish, frogs, and plants can survive until spring. If ice sank, many lakes would freeze solid from the bottom up. Next time you see a frozen pond, remember that its icy roof is actually protecting the life underneath.

For the science fair, my friend Maya and I wanted to find out which brand of paper towel soaked up the most water. We bought four kinds and cut a square of the same size from each one. Then we poured exactly 100 milliliters of water into four cups.

Our teacher, Mr. Ortiz, reminded us to change only one thing at a time. We dipped each square for ten seconds, let it drip for five seconds, and squeezed the water it held into a measuring cup. We did every test three times so that one mistake wouldn't ruin our results.

The thinnest towel held less water than we expected, but the thickest one wasn't the winner either. The best towel had a pattern of tiny pockets. We made a chart, wrote our conclusion, and learned that a good experiment needs careful steps more than lucky guesses.

Sound is a kind of energy that moves in waves. When you clap your hands, the air around them is pushed together and pulled apart very quickly. Those vibrations spread out in every direction, and when they reach your ears, your brain hears them as a clap.

In air, sound travels about 343 meters per second, which is fast, but it is much slower than light. Sound moves even faster through water and faster still through solid materials like steel. In outer space, there is no air at all, so there is nothing to carry sound waves. That is why astronauts use radios to talk to each other during a spacewalk.

An echo happens when sound bounces off a hard surface, such as a cliff or a gym wall, and returns to you. Bats and dolphins use echoes to find their food in the dark.

Every plant is made of tiny building blocks called cells, and most are far too small to see without a microscope. A plant cell has a stiff outer layer called the cell wall. It gives the plant its shape and helps stems stand up straight.

Inside the wall, there are many smaller parts, and each one has a job. The nucleus holds the cell's instructions, much like a control center. Green parts called chloroplasts capture energy from sunlight and use it to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar. This process is called photosynthesis, and it also releases the oxygen that we breathe. A large sac called a vacuole stores water. When a plant doesn't get enough water, its vacuoles shrink, and the leaves begin to droop. Give it a drink, and they fill up again.

Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, and it is often called the Red Planet. Its color comes from iron minerals in the dust and rocks, which have rusted over time. A day on Mars is only a little longer than a day on Earth, about 24 hours and 37 minutes, but a year there lasts almost twice as long as ours.

Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the largest volcano in the solar system. It is about two and a half times taller than Mount Everest. The planet also has two small moons named Phobos and Deimos, which are shaped more like potatoes than balls.

Scientists have sent many rovers to explore its surface. They have found signs that rivers and lakes once flowed there long ago. Someday, astronauts may travel to Mars and see those dry riverbeds with their own eyes.

The International Space Station circles Earth about once every 90 minutes. Because it moves so fast, the astronauts on board can see around 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day. They live and work there for months at a time, and their days are busy with experiments, repairs, and exercise.

Daily life in space can be tricky. Since everything floats, astronauts strap themselves into sleeping bags attached to the walls. They drink from pouches with straws, and they use special cups and trays so crumbs and drops won't drift into the equipment. Their muscles and bones can grow weak without gravity, so they spend about two hours a day exercising on a treadmill, a bike, and a weight machine.

Many countries work together on the station, and it has been home to astronauts from all over the world.

Dear Future Astronaut,

My name is Jordan, and I am in seventh grade. Our class is writing letters to someone who might travel to the Moon or Mars someday, so I picked you. I hope you get to see Earth from far away. Astronauts say it looks like a blue marble floating in the dark, and I think that would be the best view there is.

I have some questions for you. Is it hard to sleep when you are floating? Do you miss pizza, rain, and the smell of grass? Which do you like better, the view of Earth or the view of the stars?

When I grow up, I want to be an engineer and help build rockets. Maybe I will even help build the one you ride in. Please take a picture out the window for me, and have a safe trip there and back.

Your friend, Jordan

On a clear night, the stars seem to sparkle and flicker. They aren't really changing, though. The twinkling happens because of the air around Earth. Starlight travels for years across empty space, and then, in the last few seconds of its trip, it passes through our moving, swirling atmosphere. Pockets of warm and cool air bend the light in slightly different directions, so the star seems to jump and shimmer.

Planets usually twinkle less than stars do. A star is so far away that its light reaches us as a single tiny point, and that point is easy for the air to bend. A planet is much closer, so it looks like a small disk, and the bending tends to even out.

This is also why astronomers put telescopes on high mountains and even launch them into space, where there is less air to blur their view.

The Hawaiian Islands rose out of the Pacific Ocean one at a time, and they were all built by volcanoes. Deep under the ocean floor, there is a hot spot where melted rock pushes up toward the surface. Over many thousands of years, lava piled up until it broke through the water and formed an island.

The ocean floor is part of a huge plate that slowly moves, so each island gets carried away from the hot spot. Then a new volcano begins to grow in its place. That is why the oldest islands are in the northwest, and the youngest one, the Big Island of Hawaii, is in the southeast. Its volcano Kilauea is one of the most active in the world.

Another volcano on the Big Island, Mauna Kea, is taller than Mount Everest if you measure it from its base on the sea floor.

A glacier is a giant, slow river of ice. It forms in places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, the snow piles up and gets pressed into thick ice, and then its own weight makes it slide downhill, often just a few feet each day.

As glaciers move, they scrape and grind the land beneath them. They pick up rocks, carry them for miles, and drop them far from where they started. Long ago, during the last ice age, huge sheets of ice covered much of North America. When they melted, they left behind valleys, hills, and thousands of lakes. The Great Lakes were carved partly by glaciers, and so was the famous valley in Yosemite National Park in California.

Today, glaciers still cover parts of Alaska, Greenland, and Antarctica.

Last summer, my family drove to northern California to see the coast redwoods. I had seen pictures, but I wasn't ready for how huge they were. Some of the trees were taller than a 30-story building, and their trunks were so wide that my sister, my cousin, and I couldn't reach around one even when we held hands.

A park ranger named Ms. Lee told us that coast redwoods are the tallest trees on Earth. The tallest ones are more than 350 feet high. Their bark can be a foot thick, and it helps protect them from fires and insects. She also said that the trees get some of their water from the thick fog that rolls in from the ocean.

We walked on a trail for two hours, and it was quiet and cool the whole time. I felt smaller than an ant, but in a good way.

If you know a little about clouds, you can guess what the weather will do. Puffy white clouds that look like cotton are called cumulus clouds. They usually mean fair weather, but if they grow taller and darker during a hot afternoon, a storm may be on its way.

The tallest storm clouds are cumulonimbus clouds. They can rise more than eight miles into the sky and bring lightning, heavy rain, and sometimes hail. Flat gray clouds that cover the whole sky are stratus clouds, and they often bring drizzle or a dull, cloudy day.

High above all of these are cirrus clouds. They are thin and wispy, and they are made of ice crystals instead of water drops. When cirrus clouds spread across the sky, it can be a sign that rain or snow will arrive in a day or two. Try looking up tomorrow and naming the clouds you see.

In the 1860s, traveling from the East Coast to California could take months by wagon or ship. Many Americans dreamed of a railroad that would cross the whole country, so two companies began building one. The Central Pacific started in Sacramento, California, and laid track toward the east. The Union Pacific started near Omaha, Nebraska, and built toward the west.

The work was hard. Thousands of workers, including many immigrants from China and Ireland, blasted tunnels through mountains, built bridges, and laid rails across deserts and plains. On May 10, 1869, the two lines finally met at Promontory Summit in Utah. A golden spike was tapped into the last tie to celebrate.

After that, a trip across the country took about a week instead of several months, and the nation changed forever.

t: The Journey of Lewis and Clark
x:
In 1803, the United States bought a huge piece of land from France called the Louisiana Purchase. President Thomas Jefferson wanted to know what was there, so he asked Meriwether Lewis to lead an expedition. Lewis chose his friend William Clark to share the job, and their group became known as the Corps of Discovery.

They set out from near St. Louis in May 1804 and paddled up the Missouri River. Along the way, they made maps, collected plants, and described animals that were new to them, such as prairie dogs. A Shoshone woman named Sacagawea joined them and helped them talk with Native American nations and trade for horses.

In November 1805, the group finally reached the Pacific Ocean. They returned to St. Louis in 1806, and their maps and journals helped people learn about the West.

May 3, 1848

We left Independence, Missouri, today with our wagon, two oxen, and a cow named Daisy. Pa says the trail to Oregon is about 2,000 miles long, and it will take us until fall. Our wagon is so full of flour, bacon, tools, and quilts that there's no room to ride, so I walked beside it all day.

June 10, 1848

We crossed the Platte River this morning. The water was cold and muddy, but the oxen pulled hard, and we made it across. Tonight we camped with three other families. The children played tag while the grown-ups cooked beans and biscuits over the fire.

July 4, 1848

We reached Independence Rock today, a huge gray rock that people carve their names on. I found my uncle's name from last year! Ma let me add mine next to it.

About 4,500 years ago, the people of ancient Egypt built some of the most amazing structures in history. The Great Pyramid of Giza was made for a king named Khufu. It was built from more than two million blocks of stone, and some of them weigh more than a car. For nearly 4,000 years, it was the tallest building made by humans anywhere in the world.

Historians used to think that slaves built the pyramids, but most now believe that skilled workers and farmers did the job. Archaeologists have found the remains of their villages, bakeries, and even notes about their work crews. The workers probably used ramps, sleds, and lots of teamwork to move the heavy stones into place.

Today, the Great Pyramid is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and it is the only one still standing.

Last spring, my aunt took me to Tokyo, the capital of Japan. It's one of the largest cities in the world, and it felt busy and exciting from the moment we landed. We rode the trains everywhere, and they were so clean and on time that my aunt joked we could set our watches by them.

On our first day, we visited a park where hundreds of cherry trees were in bloom. Families sat on blankets under the pink flowers and shared picnic lunches. Then we explored a market and tried noodles, rice balls, and a sweet bean cake.

My favorite moment came on our last morning. The sky was clear, so we went to the top of a tall building, and far in the distance, I could see Mount Fuji with snow on its peak. I took more pictures of that mountain than of anything else on the whole trip.

The Amazon River in South America carries more water than any other river on Earth. It begins high in the Andes Mountains of Peru and flows east across the continent until it reaches the Atlantic Ocean in Brazil. Along the way, more than a thousand smaller rivers flow into it.

The river is surrounded by the Amazon rainforest, the largest tropical rainforest in the world. It is home to jaguars, sloths, river dolphins, and thousands of kinds of birds and fish. Many plants that grow there have never been studied by scientists.

In some places, the Amazon is so wide that you can't see the other side. There are no bridges across its main channel, so people travel by boat instead. For the towns and villages along its banks, the river is like a highway, a grocery store, and a water supply all in one.

Every place on Earth has an address made of two numbers called latitude and longitude. Lines of latitude run east and west around the globe. The most famous one is the equator, which circles the middle of the Earth at zero degrees. Places north of the equator are in the Northern Hemisphere, and places south of it are in the Southern Hemisphere.

Lines of longitude run from the North Pole to the South Pole. The starting line, called the prime meridian, passes through Greenwich, England. Places are measured in degrees east or west of it.

When you put the two numbers together, you can find any spot on a map. For example, New York City sits at about 41 degrees north and 74 degrees west. Sailors and pilots used these numbers long before phones had maps, and they still use them today.

Dear Grandma,

Greetings from Iceland! We arrived in Reykjavik on Monday, and I can't believe how different it is from home. It's the middle of June, so the sun barely sets at all. Last night, I looked out the window at midnight, and it was still as bright as early evening.

On Tuesday, we drove out to see a geyser. We waited with a crowd of people, and then it shot hot water high into the air. Everyone cheered! Iceland has lots of volcanoes, so there is hot water under the ground in many places. People even use it to heat their houses.

Yesterday, we saw a glacier, three waterfalls, and a beach with black sand. Dad says the sand is black because it came from lava. I've already filled half my sketchbook, and I'll show you all my drawings when we get back.

Love, Nora

Our family had a problem. Every Saturday, the house was a mess, and everyone argued about whose turn it was to clean. So last month, my older brother Sam and I made a chore chart. We listed every job we could think of, like washing dishes, folding laundry, feeding the dog, and taking out the trash.

Then we gave each job points. Easy jobs were worth one point, and harder jobs, like cleaning the bathroom, were worth three. Each person had to earn ten points a week. Mom liked the idea so much that she hung the chart on the fridge.

The first week was bumpy, because Dad kept forgetting to check off his jobs. By the third week, though, the house was cleaner than it had been in a long time. I even started to like vacuuming, which I never thought I would say.

Last Friday, I cooked dinner for my whole family for the first time. I chose spaghetti with tomato sauce, a green salad, and garlic bread, because those were the dishes I had watched my dad make many times.

I started early, but things still got hectic. First, I forgot to put salt in the pasta water, so I had to add it at the last minute. Then the garlic bread got a little too dark on the bottom while I was chopping cucumbers and carrots for the salad. My little sister Ava wanted to help, so I let her tear the lettuce and set the table.

When we finally sat down, everyone was quiet for a moment, and I was nervous. Then my dad said the sauce was better than his, and my mom asked for seconds. I felt proud, and I've already planned what I'll make next time.

t: How to Pack a Great Lunch
x:
Packing your own lunch can save money, and it lets you eat food you actually like. Here's a simple way to do it.

First, choose a main item that will keep you full, such as a sandwich, a wrap, or leftover pasta. Next, add a fruit and a vegetable. Apples, grapes, and clementines travel well, and so do carrot sticks and celery. Then pick a small snack, like crackers, cheese, or a handful of nuts if your school allows them.

Don't forget a drink. Water is the best choice, and a reusable bottle is better for the planet than a plastic one. If your lunch has anything that needs to stay cold, put an ice pack in your bag.

Finally, try to pack your lunch the night before. Mornings are busy, and you'll be glad it's ready when you're rushing out the door.

When my family moved to Denver in October, I had to start at a new school two months after everyone else. On my first day, I walked into the cafeteria with my tray, and every table looked full. I didn't know where to sit, so I stood there and pretended to look for someone.

Then a girl with a green backpack waved at me. Her name was Priya, and she said there was an empty seat next to her. She introduced me to her friends, Marcus and Lena, and they asked me where I was from and what kind of music I liked.

It turned out that Marcus played the trumpet in the school band, and I play the trumpet too. By the end of the week, I had joined the band, learned my way around the building, and stopped getting lost on the way to science. Now, whenever I see someone new, I try to wave first.

Basketball was invented in 1891 by a teacher named James Naismith. He worked at a school in Springfield, Massachusetts, and he needed an indoor game that would keep his students active during the cold winter. He nailed two peach baskets to the balcony of the gym, and his students tried to toss a soccer ball into them.

The first game had nine players on each team, and only one basket was scored. Every time someone made a shot, a person had to climb a ladder and get the ball out of the basket. Years later, people cut holes in the bottoms of the baskets, and eventually they switched to metal hoops and nets.

Today, basketball is played in nearly every country in the world. It's been part of the Olympic Games since 1936, and millions of kids play it in their driveways, parks, and school gyms.

Chess is a game for two players, and it's played on a board with 64 squares. Each player starts with 16 pieces: one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns. Every kind of piece moves in its own way. Bishops move diagonally, rooks move in straight lines, and knights jump in an L shape.

The goal of the game is to trap your opponent's king so it can't escape. This is called checkmate, and it ends the game right away.

When I first started playing, I lost every game to my uncle. He told me to think about three things before each move. What is my opponent trying to do? Which of my pieces are in danger? What is my best move? It took practice, but after a few months, I finally won a game. I was so excited that I asked for a rematch right away.

The score was tied at one goal each, and there were only five minutes left in the championship game. Our soccer team, the Falcons, had never won a title before. The bleachers were full of parents, grandparents, and friends, and they were all shouting at once.

Our coach called a timeout and told us to stay calm. "Pass the ball, and trust each other," she said. When the game started again, Danny stole the ball near midfield and passed it to me. I dribbled down the left side, but two defenders closed in, so I kicked the ball across the field to Rosa.

Rosa didn't waste a second. She shot the ball low, and it slid past the goalie into the corner of the net. When the final whistle blew a few minutes later, we ran onto the field and hugged. I'll remember that pass for the rest of my life.

A marathon is a race that is 26.2 miles long. According to an old Greek legend, a messenger ran from a town called Marathon all the way to Athens to share news of a victory. When the modern Olympic Games began in 1896, a long race was added to honor that story.

Runners who finish a marathon don't usually start as fast as they can. Instead, they pace themselves, which means they run at a steady speed they can keep for hours. If they start too fast, their muscles use up their stored energy early, and the last miles become much harder.

Good pacing matters in shorter races too. Track coaches often tell runners to save some energy for a strong finish. Many runners even try to run the second half of a race a little faster than the first half. It sounds hard, but it's one of the best ways to reach the finish line feeling strong.

A full orchestra can have close to 100 musicians, and they are grouped into four families. The string family is the largest. It includes violins, violas, cellos, and double basses, and they usually sit at the front of the stage. Behind them are the woodwinds, such as flutes, clarinets, oboes, and bassoons.

The brass family includes trumpets, trombones, French horns, and the tuba. Their sound is bold and bright, so they sit near the back. The percussion section has drums, cymbals, xylophones, and many other instruments that are struck or shaken.

At the front stands the conductor, who doesn't play an instrument at all. Instead, the conductor uses a thin stick called a baton to set the speed, signal when each section should come in, and shape how loudly or softly the music is played. Without the conductor, it would be hard for so many players to stay together.

In September, my best friend Elena and I decided to start a book club. We asked our librarian, Mrs. Chen, if we could meet in the library during lunch on Thursdays, and she said yes. Then we made posters and hung them in the halls.

At our first meeting, only four people came, but that was enough. We voted on our first book and picked an adventure story about a boy who survives alone in the wilderness. Everyone agreed to read the first five chapters before the next week.

The discussions were the best part. Some of us loved the main character, but others thought he made silly choices. We argued, laughed, and even changed our minds. By winter, our club had grown to eleven members. Now we take turns choosing the books, and Mrs. Chen brings snacks when someone finishes a really long one.

t: The Art of Vincent van Gogh
x:
Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch painter who lived from 1853 to 1890. He didn't start painting until he was 27 years old, but in about ten years, he created more than 2,000 works of art, including around 860 oil paintings.

His style was easy to recognize. He used bright colors, thick paint, and swirling brushstrokes that make his pictures seem to move. He loved painting ordinary things, such as sunflowers, wheat fields, cafes, and his own bedroom. One of his most famous paintings, The Starry Night, shows a sky full of glowing, spinning stars above a quiet village.

During his life, van Gogh sold very few paintings, and many people didn't understand his work. Today, though, he is one of the most admired artists in history. Visitors from all over the world travel to museums in Amsterdam, New York, and Paris to see his paintings in person.

When people watch a play, they usually see only the actors. This year, I joined the stage crew for our school's musical, and I learned how much happens behind the curtain.

For six weeks, we built the set after school. We painted a backdrop of a city skyline, built a bench that looked like it was made of stone, and hung lights above the stage. Our teacher, Mr. Davis, showed us how to use the drills safely and how to tie knots that wouldn't slip.

On opening night, I wore all black so the audience wouldn't notice me. During each scene change, I had about thirty seconds to move furniture in the dark while the music played. My heart was pounding the whole time, but every change went smoothly. When the actors took their bows, they pointed to the crew, and the audience clapped for us too.

Before the 1400s, books in Europe were copied by hand, one page at a time. It could take months to finish a single book, so books were rare and expensive. Then, around 1440, a German goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press that changed everything.

Gutenberg's big idea was movable metal type. He made small blocks for each letter, and workers arranged them to form words and pages. They inked the letters, pressed paper onto them, and then printed the same page again and again. When one page was done, they could rearrange the letters for the next.

His most famous book was a Bible printed in the 1450s. Soon, printing shops opened in cities across Europe, and books became much cheaper. More people learned to read, and new ideas spread faster than ever before.

A refrigerator doesn't really make cold. Instead, it moves heat from inside the box to the air outside it. It does this with a special liquid called a refrigerant that flows through a loop of tubes.

First, the refrigerant passes through thin coils inside the fridge. As it flows, it turns from a liquid into a gas, and that change soaks up heat from the food and air around it. Next, a pump called a compressor squeezes the gas, which makes it very hot. The hot gas then flows through coils on the back or bottom of the fridge, where it gives off its heat to the kitchen and turns back into a liquid. Then the loop starts again.

That is why the back of a refrigerator often feels warm. It's also why you should never block the vents, because the fridge needs to get rid of the heat it collects.

Orville and Wilbur Wright grew up in Dayton, Ohio, and they ran a bicycle shop there. They used the money they earned, and the skills they learned fixing bikes, to build their own flying machines. They studied birds, tested gliders, and even built a small wind tunnel to test the shapes of wings.

To find steady winds and soft sand, they traveled to Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. On December 17, 1903, Orville climbed onto their airplane, the Flyer, and took off. The flight lasted only 12 seconds, and it covered about 120 feet, which is shorter than the wingspan of many modern jets. That same day, they made three more flights, and the longest one lasted almost a minute.

It was the first time a powered airplane carried a person through the air under control, and it started the age of flight.

Many phones and tablets use a kind of touchscreen that can sense the electricity in your body. Under the glass, there is a grid of tiny wires so thin that you can't see them. The grid holds a small electric charge all the time.

When your finger touches the screen, it pulls a little of that charge toward it. The device measures where the charge changed, and then it figures out exactly where you touched. Because the grid can track many points at once, you can pinch, swipe, and zoom with two or more fingers.

This also explains why most touchscreens don't respond when you're wearing thick gloves. The fabric blocks your body's charge from reaching the screen. Some gloves have special fingertips with threads that conduct electricity, so people can use their phones on cold days without freezing their hands.
